papers.title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in Staphylococcus aureus: RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control rsaOI and rsaC, respectively. We found that rsaC, like rsaOI, is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes: lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSM and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSM production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.

papers.title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Butyrate reverts Chlamydia pneumoniae -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
papers.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extra intestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of C. pneumoniae or C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with C. trachomatis-infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated. C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping Chlamydia-host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Age Associated Shifts Toward Anaerobic Taxa and Amino Acid Degradation Potential in the Canine Oral Microbiome
papers.abstract: Introduction: Periodontal disease is common in dogs and is associated with changes in oral microbial community composition. How the canine oral microbiome restructures across age at both ecological and metabolic levels remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We analyzed shotgun metagenomic buccal-swab profiles from 1,125 dogs using MetaPhlAn. Functional profiles from HUMAnN were analyzed at pathway and functional-group levels. We annotated species-level taxa with oxygen preference and evaluated oxygen-tolerant and anaerobic taxa abundances across age. We also characterized community structure, metabolic potential, Shannon diversity, and age and weight prediction using nested cross-validated Elastic Net models. Results: Age was associated with substantial restructuring in the oral microbiome. Mean oxygen-tolerant taxa abundance decreased from 67.5% in puppies to 29.1% in mature dogs, whereas anaerobic abundance increased from 14.3% to 53.8%. The oxygen-tolerant: anaerobe log-ratio declined with age (Spearman {rho} = -0.616). Metabolic profiles also varied with age, with higher amino-acid-degradation potential and lower glycolysis and central-carbohydrate potential, and aerobic-respiration-I abundance in older dogs. Shannon diversity increased with age ({rho} = 0.537, p < 0.001). Elastic Net models trained on microbiome species abundance predicted age (Pearson r = 0.609; R-squared = 0.371) and weight (r = 0.498; R-squared = 0.248) with moderate accuracy. Discussion: Canine age was associated with coordinated changes in oral-community oxygen preference and metabolic pathways. These findings extend prior taxon-specific observations by examining a broader ecological shift and metabolic potential in the canine oral microbiome. This provides a reference for future longitudinal or clinical studies of oral maturation and periodontal disease.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding CagW, a conserved component of the Helicobacter pylori type IV secretion system, protects mice against H. pylori challenge
papers.abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

papers.title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
papers.abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence.

papers.title: A Vma13-targeted thiadiazole-succinimide disrupts V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis to block Candida albicans escape from macrophages
papers.abstract: Invasive candidiasis caused by Candida albicans is a life-threatening nosocomial infection with limited therapies and high morbidity and mortality among immunocompromised patients. Within host phagocytes, C. albicans catabolizes arginine to produce ammonia and fuels polyamine biosynthesis, which correlates with phagosomal alkalinization and yeast-to-hypha morphogenesis, facilitating macrophage escape and systemic dissemination. However, new antifungal strategies blocking this fungal escape remain scarce. Here, we characterize the thiadiazole-succinimide derivative ETSI, an arginine-dependent antifungal small molecule with minimal direct growth inhibition under arginine-free conditions yet robust anti-C. albicans activity in arginine-rich microenvironments mimicking the macrophage intracellular niche. Mechanistically, ETSI targets the vacuolar Vma13 to inhibit vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase), dissipating vacuolar proton (H+) gradients and leading to cytoplasmic H+ retention. The accumulated cytoplasmic H+ traps intracellular ammonia and blocks its external release, while impaired vacuolar metabolite sequestration further triggers cytotoxic accumulation of arginine and polyamine metabolites. This dual metabolic perturbation suppresses phagosomal alkalinization, retains C. albicans in yeast form and blocks macrophage escape. ETSI is the first small molecule blocking C. albicans escape via disrupted Vma13/V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis. This work identifies an intracellular metabolic vulnerability and establishes a niche-targeted antifungal strategy distinct from classic growth-suppressive drugs for treating invasive candidiasis.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of Helicobacter pylori infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen
papers.abstract: Background. Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories. Methods. NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of H. pylori-infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales. Results. Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR 1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5x10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions. Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.

papers.title: Systematic analysis reveals an Mln1-dependent trade-off between metabolic flexibility and thermotolerance in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: During infection, fungal pathogens must adapt to multiple environmental challenges, including changes in temperature, nutrient availability, and immune stress. Although transcriptional regulators are central to these adaptations, how individual regulators contribute to distinct environmental responses and how these responses are functionally interconnected remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functions of infection-associated transcription factors under distinct host-relevant conditions in Cryptococcus neoformans. Integrating in vivo expression profiling with infectivity data from signature-tagged mutagenesis, we prioritized 24 transcription factors, 12 of which were induced under host-mimicking conditions. Initial functional analyses revealed distinct roles for these transcription factors in adaptation to temperature, carbon, and nitrogen availability. Further characterization of Mln1, a fungal basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, uncovered an unexpected connection between carbon source adaptation and thermotolerance. Mig1-dependent repression limited MLN1 expression in the presence of glucose, whereas Mln1 accumulated in the nucleus in the presence of trehalose or ethanol, but not glucose. Loss of MLN1 impaired carbon-starvation gene expression and growth on non-preferred carbon sources, particularly trehalose. Conversely, mln1{Delta} cells accumulated more intracellular trehalose and exhibited enhanced thermotolerance, yet showed reduced melanization, titan cell formation, virulence in Drosophila, and brain fungal burden in mice. Together, these results suggest that Mln1 contributes to metabolic flexibility and fungal virulence while differentially influencing thermotolerance. More broadly, these findings highlight a potential physiological trade-off between nutrient utilization and stress resistance, suggesting that these adaptive processes may be interconnected in fungal pathogens.

papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
papers.abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

papers.title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
papers.abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

papers.title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium
papers.abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.

papers.title: YhdP forms an envelope-spanning phospholipid-binding bridge in complex with DedD
papers.abstract: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is built from phospholipids synthesised at the inner membrane, but how they cross the periplasm remains unresolved. YhdP is the leading candidate for anterograde phospholipid transfer and is predicted to form an envelope-spanning bridge. Here we purify YhdP at endogenous levels and show by cryo-electron microscopy that it contains a continuous cavity, alongside an additional density that proteomics identifies as the cell wall-binding protein DedD. Liposome co-sedimentation shows that the C-terminal helices of YhdP bind membranes directly, and single-molecule tracking reveals that endogenous YhdP is as immobile as an outer membrane protein, indicating an envelope-spanning architecture in vivo. Native mass spectrometry demonstrates that the YhdP groove accommodates all major classes of E. coli phospholipid without headgroup preference. DedD engages YhdP through its disordered region and increases lipid density at the groove entrance, suggesting a potential role in lipid loading.

papers.title: The large conjugative plasmid pAB3 integrates into the chromosome of Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 17978
papers.abstract: ATCC 17978 is one of the most utilised lab strains of Acinetobacter baumannii. Current literature suggests ATCC 17978 can have either a sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype or have the type VI secretion system (T6SS) switched on depending on the presence/absence of the large conjugative plasmid pAB3, which encodes the antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) sul2 and T6SS repressors tetR1/tetR2. Here, we show that pAB3 integrates into the ATCC 17978 chromosome, which enables a large inversion resulting in the chromosomal arrangement labelled GS2.24 by Socru. This integration has no transcriptional impact on nearby genes or tetR1/tetR2. We find several instances were a portion of integrated pAB3 containing tetR2 is lost but the rest of the sequence, including sul2, is maintained, suggesting pAB3 integration may serve to make further rearrangements more tractable, enabling a putative T6SS+ sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype.

papers.title: Lipopolysaccharide and Wzi retain capsular polysaccharide at the Klebsiella pneumoniae cell surface and promote bloodstream infection fitness
papers.abstract: Bacterial capsules are formed by individual capsular polysaccharide (CPS) polymers and are the outermost extracellular layers of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Capsules affect several aspects of bacterial biology, including resistance to host immune factors, survival in unfavorable environments and antimicrobial resistance. Research on CPS biology has largely focused on its synthesis and the pathogenic consequences of its presence or absence. Beyond synthesis, our understanding of its retention (attachment) on the cell surface is limited. Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important Gram-negative pathogen and expresses more than 80 capsular serotypes using the common Wzy-dependent CPS biosynthesis system and phenotypically manifests in various forms, making this species an attractive bacterial model to study the underexplored aspects of CPS biology. Here, we identified and characterized bacterial components involved in CPS retention in K. pneumoniae and assessed the importance of CPS retention on bloodstream fitness. Our examination revealed that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the outer-membrane protein, Wzi, collectively retain K. pneumoniae CPS on the bacterial surface. We demonstrate that the core-oligosaccharide domain of LPS and the extracellular surface of Wzi likely provide anchoring sites for CPS on the bacterial surface. Furthermore, CPS retention depends on divalent cation availability. Importantly, CPS retention on the bacterial surface is important for survival in serum and bacterial fitness at secondary infection sites in a murine bacteremia model. Together, our findings demonstrate that the functional importance of CPS to bacteria extends beyond synthesis and its overall abundance. Bacterial control over other CPS properties, like cell surface retention, are also important for K. pneumoniae fitness during bacteremia.

papers.title: Diversity-generating retroelements enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.
papers.abstract: Diversity-generating retroelements (DGRs) are genetic elements that use error-prone reverse transcription to hypermutate specific target genes, most often the receptor-binding proteins of phages. They are enriched in human gut viruses, where they are hypothesised to enable phages expand their host range. Yet DGR-mediated host-range expansion across bacterial species has so far only been predicted in silico and has not been examined directly within complex microbial communities. To test this hypothesis in situ, we tracked phage-host interactions in the human gut, combining bulk metagenomic, virus-like particle (VLP), and Hi-C sequencing of longitudinal faecal samples collected over a five-week period. This culture-independent approach identified 380 interactions between 97 phages and 76 bacterial hosts. Nearly a third of these phages (31 of 97) encoded a DGR, and DGR-encoding phages were more likely to interact with multiple bacterial species. Moreover, nucleotide diversity in DGR-targeted genes increased with the number of hosts a phage interacted with and was concentrated in the surface-exposed, DGR-targeted variable region of its receptor-binding proteins. Together, these results provide in situ evidence that DGRs enable phages to expand their host range in the human gut.

papers.title: Stream and lake network position structures freshwater microbial communities across multiple catchments
papers.abstract: Streams and lakes form hydrologically connected freshwater networks. Different environmental conditions and dispersal dynamics along the stream to lake continuum potentially affect bacterial community composition, although the strength of such effects may vary among individual catchments. Here, we analysed 224 water samples from 58 streams draining into eight lakes across Switzerland, covering the full continuum from headwaters to lake outlets. Bacterial community composition analyzed via 16S metabarcoding differed between streams and lakes, with a sharp turnover at stream and lake confluence, and this pattern was repeatable across all catchments. Lake communities had lower alpha diversity and lower overall beta dispersion than stream communities, despite hydrological connectivity with a diverse stream microbiome. Community composition in both lakes and streams differed between catchments, but this pattern was more pronounced in lakes. Lake communities were dominated by a small set of widespread and abundant core taxa, primarily established pelagic freshwater genera, that captured the catchment-level differences through shifts in relative abundance. In contrast, stream communities contained a comparatively less abundant core microbiome dominated by soil- and groundwater-associated genera, together with a larger and more diverse peripheral microbiome. Together, these findings show that bacterial community composition changes repeatably across the different positions of hydrological networks.

papers.title: CyranoPS, a novel compact temperate corynephage infecting Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001
papers.abstract: Here, we describe CyranoPS, a temperate phage isolated from the river Yvette in France, using the prophage-free strain Corynebacterium glutamicum MB001. Negative-stain electron microscopy revealed virions with siphovirus morphology. Its 14,910-bp genome has a GC content of 53.0% and 14-nt 3' overhangs at both ends. It carries 26 predicted genes, 10 without predicted functions, and no tRNAs. CyranoPS belongs to the newly established actinophage cluster ER, whose members have the smallest known genomes among Corynebacterium-infecting phages. Deletion of genes encoding the porin PorAH and the protein mycoloyltransferase MytC abolished infection, while genes encoding the mycomembrane proteins PorBC and ProtX were dispensable. CyranoPS established lysogeny in C. glutamicum through chromosomal integration probably mediated by its predicted tyrosine integrase. Integration truncated the immunity repressor gene Cyr_18, resulting in a protein devoid of its 15 C-terminal residues. The truncated repressor conferred stronger protection against superinfection than the full-length repressor. CyranoPS lysogens exhibited high levels of spontaneous prophage induction, reaching 109 PFU/mL under standard conditions, with no further increase upon treatment with mitomycin C. These findings suggest a potentially SOS-independent lytic-lysogenic switch and establish CyranoPS as a compact model to study infection and lysogeny regulation in Mycobacteriales.

papers.title: More insights into the dynamic assembly and rotation of the archaellum motor machinery
papers.abstract: Archaea use the archaellum for swimming motility. Rotation of the archaellum is driven by the ATPase ArlI and the membrane platform protein ArlJ. Structural studies suggest that conformational changes in ArlI power the rotation of ArlJ. However, how ATP hydrolysis is converted into rotation remains poorly under-stood. Using single-molecule total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, we show that dimeric ArlJ forms a complex with ArlI. Combining conservation analysis, AlphaFold3 predictions and co-purifications, we identified conserved ArlJ residues required for interaction with ArlI, including a structural-ly rigid loop and the critical residue R341 at the ArlI interface. Motility assays in Haloferax volcanii confirmed these findings. Together, these findings support a model in which a dimeric ArlJ is interacting with ArlI via conserved residues to generate torque.

papers.title: Mobile genetic elements accompany the emergence of clonal crop lineages from weed-associated populations of Xanthomonas campestris
papers.abstract: Xanthomonas campestris is a destructive pathogen of cruciferous vegetables and ornamentals and is frequently isolated from related weed species growing near agricultural land. However, the evolutionary relationships, genomic features, and biosecurity significance of weed-associated strains remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate phylogenomic and pangenomic analyses of X. campestris, including nine newly sequenced strains isolated from invasive garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata), to compare strains from cultivated and non-cultivated hosts across multiple pathovars. Weed-isolated strains predominantly clustered within basal, genetically diverse lineages associated with broad host ranges, whereas crop-isolated strains were concentrated in host-associated clonal lineages. The emergence of specialized crop-associated lineages coincided with multiple inferred acquisitions of large mobile elements, including integrative conjugative and mobilizable elements and plasmids carrying genes previously associated with pathogenicity and host range. Although these elements were enriched in clonal crop-associated lineages, they also occurred in diverse weed-associated strains, indicating that genetic material associated with crop infection is distributed among divergent lineages and persists in wild and weedy systems. These findings identify invasive weeds as ancillary hosts that may harbor pathogen diversity and provide opportunities for genetic exchange, underscoring the importance of surveillance beyond agricultural fields to monitor pathogen diversification and emerging threats. Our pangenomic analysis also identified crop-associated pathogen factors and putative host resistance targets for future investigation, providing a foundation for developing critically needed black rot-resistant cultivars.

papers.title: oidyPeaks: R package for automated flow cytometry cell cycle analysis and visualization in fungal microbes
papers.abstract: Karyotypic variation in fungal populations from ecological, clinical, and industrial environments and is also a hallmark of many cancers. The evolutionary dynamics of karyotypic vriants (i.e., changes in the number of chromosomes, either as complete sets or single chromosomes) are the same as any de novo mutation. To quantify karyotypic subpopulations within evolving populations, an unbiased computational method is required to identify subpopulations and quantify their abundance. Flow cytometry is the standard method to measure the genome size from large populations of individual cells. Cell populations typically include cells in all stages of the cell cycle (G0/G1 before DNA replication, S phase during replication, and G2/M after DNA replication but before cell division). Existing mathematical models can be fit to genome-size distributions to determine the base ploidy of a population, but existing algorithms assume a single base ploidy. Mixed-karyotype populations therefore require manual gating to subdivide the flow cytometry data before analysis, which introduces bias, as it is not always clear where or when gates should be drawn. To overcome this, we developed a new method that identifies and quantifies karyotypic subpopulations from flow cytometry data. The open-source R package ploidyPeaks builds on existing Bioconductor tools to import and manipulate standard .fcs flow cytometry files. Using reference populations of known ploidy, we established thresholds to distinguish single-genome size populations and identify candidate mixed-karyotype samples. We then developed a peak-detection algorithm to identify G0/G1 and G2/M peaks, resolve karyotypic subpopulations within mixed populations, and apply nonlinear least-squares fitting of the Dean-Jett-Fox cell-cycle model to each subpopulation, providing a confidence measure for model fit. Compared with existing methods, our approach quantifies genome size in mixed-karyotype populations without manual intervention while providing an objective measure of model fit. We demonstrate the utility of this method on 240 replicate populations initiated from 20 Candida albicans genetic backgrounds evolving for 100 generations to the antifungal drug fluconazole.

papers.title: Enhanced Antimicrobial Potency and Therapeutic Index of a Defined C12 Quaternary Ammonium Compound
papers.abstract: Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) remain a major clinical burden and are complicated by antimicrobial resistance, polymicrobial infections, and biofilm-mediated therapeutic tolerance. Topical antimicrobials can provide localized activity while reducing systemic exposure, but currently available agents are limited by narrow spectra, cytotoxicity, poor antibiofilm activity, and resistance development. We evaluated C12-alkyl(ethylbenzyl)dimethyl ammonium chloride (EQ12), a next-generation quaternary ammonium compound, in vitro as a topical antimicrobial candidate for leading bacterial causes of SSTIs. Broth microdilution assays were used to determine minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and minimum bactericidal concentrations (MBCs) against methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Species-selective plating was used to assess bactericidal activity in staphylococcal-P. aeruginosa co-cultures. Crystal violet assays quantified biofilm inhibition against MRSA, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii, and serial passage experiments assessed resistance emergence over 14 passages. EQ12 inhibited all species tested, with MICs of 2.3 to 40 micrograms/mL and MBCs of 4.7 to 40 micrograms/mL. EQ12 outperformed benzalkonium chloride and povidone-iodine against Gram-negative isolates and retained bactericidal activity in mixed cultures, although staphylococcal susceptibility decreased in the presence of P. aeruginosa. EQ12 inhibited biofilm formation at sub-MIC to near-MIC concentrations and did not induce resistance in MRSA, P. aeruginosa, or A. baumannii, unlike comparator topical antibiotics. These findings support further development of EQ12 as a topical antimicrobial for SSTI-associated pathogens.

papers.title: A bacterial chaperone-usher pathway links interkingdom association to antimicrobial protection of a fungal partner
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial compounds (AMCs) influence species-level composition of microbial communities, governing beneficial and pathogenic interactions with plant and mammalian hosts. Phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (PCA) is a bacterially produced, redox-active AMC abundant in the rhizosphere. A recent study discovered the PCA-susceptible fungus Aspergillus calidoustus can grow in PCA-abundant environments by associating with phenazine-tolerant bacteria, including the novel species Paraburkholderia edwinii. P. edwinii's protection response is characterized by adherence to its fungal partner, bacterial aggregation, and sequestration and reduction of PCA, rendering PCA less toxic. Deletion of the bacterial transcriptional repressor HrcA generates a constitutively active protection response and enhanced protection of A. calidoustus. Here, we use the {Delta}hrcA strain to determine whether fungal protection uses bacterial self-protection machinery or dedicated interkingdom mechanisms. We identified a divergent archaic chaperone-usher pathway (CUP) operon encoding a predicted periplasmic chaperone, outer membrane usher, putative major pilin-like subunit, and putative adhesin-like tip protein. While many archaic CUP operons are annotated in diverse bacteria, their functions remain largely unexplored. We show these fungal attachment complex ( fac ) genes promote bacterial-fungal attachment, are required for P. edwinii to sequester and detoxify PCA, and contribute to full fungal protection from PCA stress, despite not being required for P. edwinii's own tolerance of PCA. We further identified the transcription regulator, FacR, that influences expression of the fac system. Understanding the functions of divergent archaic CUP systems may illuminate protective interkingdom partnerships and inform how pathogenic and beneficial microbes gain entry to AMC-replete environments, shaping microbial communities in agricultural and clinical contexts.

papers.title: Molecular characterization of thermo-adapted Novirhabdovirus variants and virulence in vivo in rainbow trout and zebrafish at different temperatures.
papers.abstract: Controlling viral diseases in fish is a challenge for the sustainable development of aquaculture and improving the health of fish farms. Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is a major pathogen in aquaculture. It infects cold-water fish, but loses its infectivity at temperatures above 20{degrees}C. Since fish are poikilothermic animals, their body temperature fluctuates according to that of their environment. Faced with current climate change, it is crucial to understand how these pathogens will adapt to rising temperatures. Through a strategy simulating the impact of global warming, this virus has been progressively thermo-adapted to 25{degrees}C. The selected variant, IHNV25, replicates at 25{degrees}C while maintaining efficient replication at low temperatures, like its parental strain. Genome sequencing and a reverse genetics approach revealed that only 9 amino acid substitutions, distributed across 4 of the 6 viral genes, were essential for thermo-adaptation. Although IHNV25 was highly attenuated in its natural host, the rainbow trout, at any temperatures, it proved highly virulent when injected in zebrafish larvae at 20{degrees}C and 25{degrees}C, inducing severe symptoms identical to those observed in trout (hemorrhages, oedema, and exophthalmia). At both temperatures, mortality was preceded by a massive viral replication and a delayed and inefficient interferon and inflammatory response. Unlike the parental strain, IHNV25 was also capable of infecting larvae by bath immersion at 25{degrees}C, entering via the caudal fin, thus demonstrating its ability to cross the species barrier. The identification of viral markers of thermo-adaptation will therefore be of great interest for the epidemiological surveillance of field isolates.

papers.title: Structure-activity relationship study in soil identifies an effective broad-spectrum inhibitor of archaeal nitrification
papers.abstract: Ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) can contribute substantially to nitrification in agricultural soils, yet the portfolio of AOA-targeting nitrification inhibitors (NIs) with demonstrated efficacy under soil conditions remains limited. Moreover, the performance of candidate inhibitors in soil is often difficult to predict from pure-culture assays because their activity is strongly influenced by soil-dependent factors. In this study, we employed a recently developed high-throughput miniaturized soil incubation assay to perform a soil-based structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis of SIAS (Specific Inhibitor of AOA in Soil), a pyrazolo-pyridine derivative previously identified as an AOA-targeting compound with strong additive nitrification inhibition effects when combined with the AOB-targeting inhibitor DMP (3,4-dimethyl-1H-pyrazole). To identify structural features associated with improved and more robust soil efficacy, a library of 27 SIAS-derived pyrazolo-pyridine analogues was evaluated directly in soil. The SAR analysis showed that inhibitory activity was governed by a specific combination of structural features and led to the discovery of Optimized SIAS (Opt. SIAS), a simplified analogue that consistently outperformed the original lead compound across diverse agricultural soils. Correlation analysis further revealed that soil pH and, particularly, silt content were major determinants of Opt. SIAS efficacy. The strong additive effects obtained through combined application of Opt. SIAS and DMP highlight the contribution of AOA to residual nitrification following AOB inhibition and demonstrate the potential of simultaneously targeting both groups. Together, these results expand the limited portfolio of effective AOA-targeting nitrification inhibitors and provide a foundation for the development of next-generation nitrification inhibition strategies aimed at improving nitrogen-use efficiency and reducing nitrogen losses from agricultural soils.

papers.title: CpxR-CpxS two-component system exacerbates development of antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as a member of the ESKAPE pathogens, is well known for its ability to develop multidrug resistance following antibiotic therapy. Overexpression of the efflux pumps, often caused by dysfunction of related transcriptional factors, is well known as a common mechanism underpins multidrug resistance. Previous work showed direct regulatory link of CpxR-CpxS, an OmpR-EnvZ family two-component system, with the expression of the predominant MexAB-OprM efflux pump in P. aeruginosa. However, the contribution of this regulatory link to the development of antibiotic resistance has not been fully elucidated. In this work, it has been shown that deletion of cpxR, but not cpxS, reduces the emergence of multidrug resistant colonies almost 1000 times lower compared to the parental wild type P. aeruginosa PA14 following sub-lethal antibiotic exposure, suggesting that apart from CpxS, other sensory component(s) or pathway(s) can also mediate CpxR activity in the development of antibiotic resistance in P. aeruginosa. We further demonstrate that when glucose is used as the sole carbon source, it leads to increased expression levels of mexA and reduced antibiotics susceptibilities in the PA14{Delta}cpxS strain in a cpxR dependent manner. GtrS, another EnvZ family sensor kinase, but not the well-known AckA-Pta pathway, mediates this glucose effects. Both in vivo and in vitro evidences support that GtrS can activate CpxR in a cross-talk manner in the absence of CpxS. Besides gtrS, at least four other sensor kinase genes (envZ, tctE, phoR and colS) can exert activation effect upon CpxR in the PA14{Delta}cpxS strain. Having the risk of multiple way to antibiotic resistance development, cpxS null mutations can be emerged in P. aeruginosa clinical isolates. Since many OmpR-EnvZ family two-component system have been shown to be engaged in antibiotic resistance, its potential risk of exacerbating antibiotic resistance in ESKAPE pathogens has been discussed.

papers.title: A broadly active flavivirus NS4B targeting compound that blocks NS4B-NS3 binding and replication organelle formation
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne orthoflaviviruses, including West Nile virus (WNV), dengue virus (DENV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), cause substantial global morbidity and mortality, yet no broadly effective direct-acting antivirals are available. The viral nonstructural protein NS4B has emerged as a promising antiviral target, although the compounds described to date are largely DENV-specific. Here we characterize SRI-38841, a xanthine analog derived from hit-to-lead optimization of a previously described WNV inhibitor, which inhibits WNV replication with an IC90 of 0.87 {micro}M and low cytotoxicity, and retains activity against DENV, ZIKV, and JEV. Serial passage of WNV under compound selection yielded resistant viruses bearing mutations in NS4B, and reverse genetics was used to confirm the role of individual amino acid substitutions. Several of these residues map to regions analogous to those implicated in resistance to the DENV NS4B inhibitors JNJ-A07 and NITD-688. Docking of SRI-38841 to an AlphaFold2 model of WNV NS4B predicted a binding pocket within a cytosolic-facing funnel, and mutation of the pocket residues A45 and K56 likewise conferred resistance, while changes at Q170 and T220 did not. Together, these data favor a topology model in which the compound engages a cytosolic-facing pocket over one placing these residues in the ER lumen. Mechanistically, SRI-38841 disrupts the NS4B-NS3 interaction and abolishes replication organelle formation in infected cells. Unlike JNJ-A07 and NITD-688, which were inactive against WNV and ZIKV, SRI-38841 inhibits all four viruses tested, identifying this xanthine class as a starting point for broadly active orthoflavivirus antivirals.

papers.title: Iron as a critical determinant for survival, oxidative stress, and infectivity of Leishmania parasites
papers.abstract: Iron is an essential for all living organisms, including humans, and is present in RBCs & other iron-binding proteins that play crucial roles in oxygen transport, DNA synthesis & electron transport. Similarly, iron also plays a critical role in parasite biology. The unicellular Leishmania parasites scavenge essential iron inside host macrophages. We investigated the impact of iron on parasite growth, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and the expression of proteins involved in ROS, thiol metabolism, Fe-S clusters, and infectivity in macrophages. Our findings revealed that optimum iron concentrations promote parasite proliferation, whereas higher levels induce toxicity, leading to DNA fragmentation and caspase-like activity. Iron supplementation enhances parasite tolerance to oxidative stress by decreasing intracellular ROS and increasing total intracellular thiol content in a concentration-dependent manner. However, iron depletion increases ROS levels and decreases total thiol content in a concentration-dependent manner, which disrupts redox homeostasis. To support our finding, we further exposed these treated parasites to menadione, which supports that iron-supplemented cells can better survive under oxidative stress than the depleted cells. Furthermore, extra iron availability increases the expression of key metabolic proteins, Fe-S clusters (Nbp35, Frataxin, IScU) and thiol metabolism (TryS, TryR, CS, SAT, cTXN, cTXNPx), while under iron-depleted conditions these proteins were downregulated except frataxin. In vitro infectivity demonstrated that iron supplementation enhances parasite infectivity, while iron depletion impairs percentage infectivity. Our study demonstrates the roles of iron in the survival, redox regulation, and virulence of L. donovani, which can correlate with the role of cellular iron homeostasis in VL pathogenesis.

papers.title: Phosphatidylserine receptors are critical for lethal infection by Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus
papers.abstract: The tick-borne Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) causes severe and often fatal hemorrhagic disease for which no approved countermeasures are available. Herein, we identify the phosphatidylserine receptors (PSRs) AXL, TIM-1, and TIM-4 as critical entry host factors for CCHFV in cell lines and liver-derived primary cell cultures. Small-molecule and antibody-based PSR inhibitors greatly reduced viral infection in cell culture. Germline knockout of individual PSR genes afforded partial protection against CCHFV infection, disease, and death in a murine model of lethal viral challenge. Mice engineered to lack two PSRs were completely protected from challenge, with viremia and viral replication, pathology, and inflammation in the liver and spleen reduced to baseline. Therefore, PSRs are collectively indispensable for CCHFV infection and pathogenesis. We conclude that PSRs are not just cell entry factors but bona fide determinants of infection, dissemination, and disease by CCHFV and legitimate targets for the development of new antiviral countermeasures.
